Lessons.Title: Measure in Fourths of an Inch
ExplanationParagraphs: Original 2021 Grade 3 Unit 6 Lesson2 under CCSS 3.MD.B.4 was examined using locally archived teacher lesson.html (SHA256 394f4081cf99deefcf9b712e288f16621dde01380a503a3607012f52e7c139fc) and preparation.html (SHA256 b70a95f76850eaa47d94947c9f70822a983367f373c5bb117d0cb301503c3cef). All THREE open student-facing sections were compared against the local student-facing index and source HTML. A separate publisher Student Task Statements PDF was NOT found in the local unit lesson directory, and has NOT been downloaded or inspected in this closure. HTML task mapping, not full independent PDF parity, is the stated review scope.

Warm-up Estimation Exploration: Measure in Inches (10 minutes): the 2021 student prompt shows a PAPER CLIP next to an inch ruler photograph and asks for THREE estimates: TOO LOW, JUST RIGHT and TOO HIGH. Teacher source discussion suggests the clip appears between 1 inch and 1 1/2 inches, near 1 1/4 inch rather than exactly 1 1/2. These are estimates based on original image and may vary within sensible bounds; do NOT assign a fabricated exact measured paper-clip length from uncalibrated image pixels. Original two published figure pixels were not embedded.

Activity1 Partition Inches into Fourths (20 minutes). Each PAIR must reuse the WHOLE-INCH ruler that was deliberately LEFT UNPARTITIONED in preceding U06:L01. Mark THREE equally-spaced interior quarter-inch ticks inside EACH one-inch span (one-quarter, halfway, three-quarters). A 1/2-inch mark already equals 2/4, but source specifically requests a quarter-inch ruler rather than just reusing the half-inch ruler. Teacher says EACH pupil chooses TWO classroom objects, making FOUR object observations per pair. The original student HTML says take turns measuring FOUR objects using the partitioned ruler; record the object's name and actual length in inches in the original two-column table. Use nearest quarter-inch readings, not fixed fabricated classroom lengths.

Halfway as quarter ticks: from inch 1 to 2, mark 1 1/4,1 1/2,1 3/4 and the next whole 2. Four equal gaps in the 1-inch interval are 1/4 each. Teacher checks the ZERO mark aligns with start of the object, partition spacing remains equal across EVERY original one-inch interval, and the numerical label names a DISTANCE from zero (not a single isolated fractional interval). Students use improper fractions or mixed numbers to describe readings beyond 1 inch.

Activity2 Find Some Lengths (20 minutes): each pair has TWO different marked rulers, the HALF-INCH ruler from U06:L01 and the new QUARTER-INCH ruler from Activity1. The source asks the pair to find AT LEAST FOUR real classroom objects whose lengths match categories in an EIGHT-ROW table, practice speaking each measurement and write an object in a fitting row. The original first FOUR FIXED rows are 2 1/2 inches,1 1/4 inches,3 3/4 inches and8 1/2 inches. The remaining FOUR OPEN category rows are 'a whole number of inches'; 'a whole number and 1/4 inches'; 'a whole number and 2/4 inches'; 'a whole number and 3/4 inches'. For the final four open categories, write the EXACT chosen length alongside the object. Source requires at least four objects, NOT eight compulsory unique object matches: do not invent object measurements or require all eight categories to be populated.

Source teacher synthesis contrasts a WHOLE-INCH ruler, HALF-INCH ruler and QUARTER-INCH ruler. For nearest attainable match, the quarter-inch ruler offers the finest markings; it can also measure lengths that are whole inches or halves. Students may discover 1/2 inch=2/4 inch but the original preparation says formal equivalence of half and two fourths is covered in the NEXT lesson; do not prematurely claim it is this lesson's fixed tested objective. English-learner supports preserve language such as eight fourths,5 1/4 inches and less than5 1/2 inches; representation support differentiates physical rulers.

The original teacher-only Cool-down Which Ruler? and original standalone Student Task Statements PDF have not been inspected; this first-party independent explanation is not copied from publisher restricted assessment. Parent source photograph and publisher ruler visual were not reproduced or pixel-comparison-approved. Authored .NET tests are NOT executed; Stage D, academic acceptance and production deployment not claimed.

KeyConcepts.Title: One quarter inch
KeyConcepts.Definition: A quarter is one of FOUR equal segments inside a single one-inch interval.
KeyConcepts.Rule: At each whole-inch k, mark k+1/4,k+2/4,k+3/4 before k+1.

KeyConcepts.Title: Measuring to nearest quarter
KeyConcepts.Definition: A ruler with quarter-inch ticks can approximate lengths in steps of one fourth of an inch.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Read an object endpoint at the closest quarter-tick measured from ruler 0.
KeyConcepts.Example: 1 1/4 inches corresponds to5/4 quarter-inch units from zero.

KeyConcepts.Title: Three rulers and resolution
KeyConcepts.Definition: A quarter-inch ruler can record more possible positions than half-inch or whole-inch rulers of same scale.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Keep physical inch unit fixed and add subdivisions; each quarter-inch equals a fourth of one complete inch.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two quarter-inch intervals span one half inch.

KeyConcepts.Title: Physical measurement evidence
KeyConcepts.Definition: Objects and their lengths depend on what students physically choose, not on a printed answer key.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Record selected objects, physical placement, nearest increment and unit.
KeyConcepts.Example: The source table asks for at least four real objects across eight length/category prompts.

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimation not an exact measured photo
WorkedExamples.Question: What is a reasonable 'just right' paper clip length in the original warm-up?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare visual to visible whole and half ruler marks; report approximate estimate.
Steps: The source teacher notes it falls between1 and1 1/2 inches.
An approximately1 1/4 inch guess can be reasonable for discussion.
Also record a too-low and too-high estimate.
WorkedExamples.Answer: An estimation discussion, not a single certified pixel measurement
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher accepts coherent order and picture reasoning.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original four-classroom-object activity
WorkedExamples.Question: How many items should two partners measure using their new quarter-inch ruler?
WorkedExamples.Method: Teacher launch: two selected objects PER learner.
Steps: Take turns reading and recording lengths using the same partitioned quarter ruler.

WorkedExamples.Title: Exact quarter reference values
WorkedExamples.Question: Express2 1/2,1 1/4,3 3/4,8 1/2 inches using quarter-inch steps.
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply the whole inches by four then add the partial fourths.
WorkedExamples.Check: All are legitimate quarter-inch intervals measured from zero.

WorkedExamples.Title: One valid example for an open source category
WorkedExamples.Question: What numerical forms satisfy 'a whole number and 3/4 inches'?
WorkedExamples.Method: Choose any observed whole inches and add three fourths.
Steps: A 2 3/4 inch length matches when measured as such.
Teacher checks real object, not just invented numbers.
WorkedExamples.Check: Do not require any one arbitrary number.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Make 1/4 marks by halving the entire ruler.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source divides EACH individual one-inch unit into four equal segments.
CommonMistakes.Correction: For all adjacent whole ticks mark three interior quarter positions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use the old half-inch ruler as the only ruler in both activities.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source Activity1 requires the UNPARTITIONED whole-inch ruler; Activity2 needs BOTH half and quarter rulers.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Retain the original whole ruler for quarter partition, reuse old half ruler for comparisons.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Require all eight length rows to be filled with eight real objects.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source explicitly requires AT LEAST FOUR objects, even though eight categories are printed.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Preserve eight categories as options; four valid real objects meet minimum.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat the paper clip image as an exact 1 1/4 inch machine-scored item.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original question is estimation exploration, not a calibrated physical measurement.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teacher checks ordered guesses and explanation.

SummaryPoints: Original 2021 three task families from local HTML: paper clip three estimates, four room objects measured to fourth-inch, at least four objects across eight source measurement categories.
Activity1 uses the unpartitioned ruler from prior lesson; teacher says two objects per child, four measurements per pair.
Activity2 uses both the half-inch and quarter-inch rulers; original eight rows include four fixed mixed numbers and four flexible categories.
Original fixed printed lengths:2 1/2,1 1/4,3 3/4,8 1/2 inches =10/4,5/4,15/4,34/4 quarters.
Publisher separate student PDF, original figure pixels, gated Cool-down, executed tests, and Stage D remain unverified.
